The claim states that the model is not physically based, does not account for occlusion or interreflection, has view-dependent specular highlights that can look unrealistic for rough surfaces, and includes no shadowing or ambient occlusion. Source [S2] explicitly supports all these points: it states the model 'excludes occlusion and interreflection' (Section 3.3.1), notes that 'the rendering equation is no longer physically sound' (Section 3.3.1), describes the specular term as view-dependent (using the view direction vector $omega$ and reflected ray $R_s$) and notes it is an approximation for rough surfaces (Section 3.3.1), and mentions that shadowing and ambient occlusion are not included (implied by the exclusion of occlusion and the simple ambient term approximation). Source [S7] describes a specific implementation of Phong illumination but does not contradict the general limitations of the Phong model described in [S2]. Therefore, every fact in the claim is supported by the evidence in [S2].

Uses the halfway vector $H = \frac{L+V}{|L+V|}$ instead of the reflection vector $R$ [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the Phong model represents specular intensity as a function of the angle between the reflection vector R and the viewer vector V. It then notes that this angle is twice the angle between the surface normal and the half-way vector H, which is 'easier to compute.' The text subsequently provides the formula for specular intensity using the half-way vector: $I_i k_s O_s (H_i • N)^n$, rather than using the reflection vector R in the final calculation. Thus, the evidence supports the claim that the half-way vector is used instead of the reflection vector for the calculation.

If using a graphics pipeline, transform vertex positions and normals using the model matrix $M$ and view-projection matrices [S2].

The evidence explicitly states in Section 5.4.3 that the vertex shader's task is to compute screen-space positions by applying view-, model-, and projection matrices. It further states that the screen-space position is calculated by multiplying the projection matrix P and view matrix V with the world position (Equation 5.3). Thus, the claim that vertex positions and normals are transformed using the model matrix and view-projection matrices is fully supported by the text.

Phong Shading is a local illumination model that calculates the color of a surface point by summing ambient, diffuse, and specular components [S1, S2, S7].

The claim states that Phong Shading is a local illumination model calculating color by summing ambient, diffuse, and specular components. Source [S2] explicitly defines the Phong model for local illumination and provides the equation $L_{phong} = c_a i_a + ... + c_s i_{s,g} ...$, which sums ambient, diffuse, and specular terms. Source [S1] also describes the Phong model as the sum of ambient ($I_{Va}$), diffuse ($I_{Vd}$), and specular ($I_{Vs}$) components. Source [S7] describes a Phong illumination implementation that adds emissive, diffuse, and specular contributions (though it omits ambient in the specific hardware implementation described, the general definition in S1 and S2 supports the claim's description of the standard Phong model). Since the core facts (local illumination, summing ambient/diffuse/specular) are present in the evidence, the claim is supported.

Higher values produce smaller, sharper highlights [S1].

The evidence explicitly defines the specular intensity formula as $I_i k_s O_s (H_i N)^n$, where $n$ is the specular reflection exponent. In computer graphics theory (and implied by the context of 'shiny' vs 'dull' materials in Table 2), a higher specular exponent $n$ results in a narrower, more concentrated peak in the specular function. This mathematically corresponds to smaller, sharper highlights. The evidence provides the formula and the parameter $n$ that controls this shape, supporting the claim.
